## Regression Benchmark: Kin8nm {#sec-kin8nm}

The two financial risk classification experiments in @sec-credit-risk (presented next) show that DGPs do not meaningfully outperform single-layer GPs on credit-default surfaces, which are approximately smooth and monotonic. A natural question is whether the additional compositional flexibility of DGPs can yield measurable gains on data with genuinely non-stationary, hierarchical structure. To test this, we first evaluate the same GP and DGP architectures on the Kin8nm dataset — a standard regression benchmark from the UCI repository that has been widely used in the DGP literature [@salimbeni_doubly_2017; @damianou_deep_2013].

Kin8nm contains 8,192 observations of the forward kinematics of an 8-link robot arm. The eight input features are joint angles, and the target is the distance of the end-effector from a desired position. The mapping from joint angles to end-effector position is a composition of trigonometric transformations — precisely the kind of hierarchical non-linearity where intermediate representations should help. This makes Kin8nm an ideal test case for whether the DGP architecture adds value when the data structure warrants it.

### Experimental Design

The 8,192 observations were split into a fixed test set of 1,639 observations (20%) with the remaining 6,553 observations forming the development pool. Three training tiers were evaluated:

- **Small** ($N_{\text{dev}} = 500$): 425 training, 75 validation.
- **Medium** ($N_{\text{dev}} = 3{,}000$): 2,550 training, 450 validation.
- **Large** ($N_{\text{dev}} = 6{,}553$): 5,570 training, 983 validation (full development set).

All features were standardised to zero mean and unit variance, fit on training data only. The model set mirrors the classification experiments: Ridge Regression, Random Forest (500 trees), XGBoost (with early stopping), SVGP (512 inducing points, 150 epochs), DSVGP-2L (128 inducing points per layer, hidden dimension 5), and DSVGP-3L. GP and DGP models use a Gaussian likelihood for regression. Classical models do not provide predictive variances, so NLPD (negative log predictive density) is reported only for the GP family.

### Results at Full Scale {#sec-kin8nm-large}

| Model | RMSE | MAE | R² | NLPD | Time (s) |
|:------|:----:|:---:|:--:|:----:|:--------:|
| Ridge Regression | 0.2023 | 0.1626 | 0.408 | — | 0.001 |
| Random Forest | 0.1435 | 0.1131 | 0.702 | — | 2.30 |
| XGBoost | 0.1190 | 0.0902 | 0.795 | — | 1.70 |
| SVGP | 0.0783 | 0.0601 | 0.911 | $-1.116$ | 40.5 |
| **DSVGP-2L** | **0.0699** | **0.0541** | **0.929** | $\mathbf{-1.241}$ | 35.9 |
| DSVGP-3L | 0.0759 | 0.0583 | 0.917 | $-1.158$ | 147.5 |

: Regression results on Kin8nm at full scale ($N_{\text{train}} = 5{,}570$, $N_{\text{test}} = 1{,}639$). Bold entries indicate best values. Lower RMSE, MAE, and NLPD are better; higher R² is better. {#tbl-kin8nm-large}

![Predicted vs actual values at full scale. DSVGP-2L shows the tightest clustering around the diagonal, with RMSE = 0.0699 vs SVGP's 0.0783.](/sections/4-modeling/assets/kin8nm/large/predicted_vs_actual.png){#fig-kin8nm-pred-actual}

The Kin8nm results present a qualitatively different picture from the financial datasets. DSVGP-2L achieves RMSE = 0.0699 versus SVGP's 0.0783 — a **10.7% reduction** — and R² = 0.929 versus 0.911. The NLPD improvement ($-1.241$ vs $-1.116$) indicates that the DGP not only predicts more accurately but also provides better-calibrated predictive uncertainty. This is the first dataset across our experiments where additional GP depth translates into a clear and consistent performance gain.

The improvement aligns with the theoretical expectation: Kin8nm's target is a composition of trigonometric functions of the joint angles, creating a non-stationary surface where the function's local behaviour changes across the input space. The DGP's hidden layer learns an intermediate representation — effectively a warping of the input space — that makes the final-layer mapping smoother and easier to model [@damianou_deep_2013]. A single RBF kernel with fixed lengthscales cannot adapt to the varying smoothness across different joint-angle configurations, limiting the single-layer SVGP's accuracy.

DSVGP-3L (RMSE = 0.0759) is worse than DSVGP-2L, consistent with the pattern across all three datasets that a third layer adds optimisation difficulty without commensurate expressiveness gains.

### Scaling Behaviour {#sec-kin8nm-scaling}

| Model | RMSE (S) | RMSE (M) | RMSE (L) | R² (S) | R² (M) | R² (L) |
|:------|:-------:|:-------:|:-------:|:------:|:------:|:------:|
| Ridge Regression | 0.2040 | 0.2025 | 0.2023 | 0.398 | 0.408 | 0.408 |
| Random Forest | 0.1884 | 0.1607 | 0.1435 | 0.487 | 0.627 | 0.702 |
| XGBoost | 0.1826 | 0.1389 | 0.1190 | 0.518 | 0.721 | 0.795 |
| SVGP | 0.1742 | 0.0844 | 0.0783 | 0.562 | 0.897 | 0.911 |
| DSVGP-2L | 0.2011 | 0.0885 | **0.0699** | 0.416 | 0.887 | **0.929** |
| DSVGP-3L | 0.2628 | 0.0887 | 0.0759 | 0.002 | 0.886 | 0.917 |

: RMSE and R² scaling across training tiers. S = small (425 train), M = medium (2,550 train), L = large (5,570 train). {#tbl-kin8nm-scaling}

The scaling behaviour confirms the data-efficiency pattern observed on the financial datasets. At small scale, SVGP leads (RMSE = 0.1742) while DSVGP-2L (0.2011) and DSVGP-3L (0.2628) lag behind — the deeper architectures cannot learn useful intermediate representations from 425 observations. DSVGP-3L's R² = 0.002 at small scale again demonstrates the pathological near-constant prediction failure of overly deep architectures in the low-data regime [@duvenaud_avoiding_2014].

At medium scale, the gap closes: SVGP = 0.0844, DSVGP-2L = 0.0885, DSVGP-3L = 0.0887. At full scale, DSVGP-2L overtakes SVGP decisively. This crossover — DGPs underperforming with limited data but outperforming at sufficient scale — is the key empirical finding: **depth helps when there is both sufficient data and genuinely compositional structure in the target function**.
